Broken access control is the number one risk on the OWASP Top 10.

Scanners rarely catch it. The server hands the wrong user's data back with a 200 OK, and nothing looks broken.

What to do this week:
1. Log in as two users. Can one open the other's records?
2. Test every API endpoint, not just the pages.

Source: OWASP Top 10:2025

43% of UK businesses had a cyber breach or attack in the last 12 months.

This isn't just big corporates. Among small businesses the figure was 46%.

What to do this week:
1. Turn on MFA for email and admin accounts.
2. Find out what you have exposed to the internet.

Source: Cyber Security Breaches Survey 2025/26, GOV.UK

Phishing hit 38% of UK businesses in a single year.

It's still the most common attack by far. One convincing email is often the whole way in.

What to do this week:
1. Run a short phishing session with your staff.
2. Make reporting a dodgy email quick and blame-free.

Source: Cyber Security Breaches Survey 2025/26, GOV.UK

Ransomware is now present in 44% of breaches.

Attacks rose 37% in a year. Backups you've actually tested to restore are worth more than any promise.

What to do this week:
1. Keep an offline backup and test a restore.
2. Patch internet-facing systems first.

Source: Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report 2025

Only 25% of UK businesses have a formal incident response plan.

If you're breached tomorrow morning, who makes the first call? Decide that before you need to.

What to do this week:
1. Write a one-page plan: who does what, and when.
2. Keep key contact numbers somewhere offline.

Source: Cyber Security Breaches Survey 2025/26, GOV.UK

What to do this week:

Under UK GDPR you have 72 hours to report a notifiable breach to the ICO.

The clock starts when you become aware of it. Know who does what before it starts ticking.

What to do this week:
1. Name who decides if a breach is reportable.
2. Keep the ICO reporting steps in your plan.

Source: ICO, Personal data breaches: a guide

Only 15% of UK businesses review the cyber risk from their immediate suppliers.

Your data is only as safe as the weakest company that holds it.

What to do this week:
1. List every supplier with access to your data.
2. Ask them how they protect it.

Source: Cyber Security Breaches Survey 2025/26, GOV.UK
